Enphase Energy Announces IQ Meter Collar Approval by 80 Utilities in the U.S. and Canada
FREMONT, Calif., Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today announced that the Enphase® IQ® Meter Collar is now approved for behind-the-meter installation by 80 utilities that collectively serve more than 38 million customers across the United States and Canada.
The IQ Meter Collar is now approved by all three major investor-owned electric utilities in California and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), expanding access to whole-home backup across the state. Hawaiian Electric has also approved initial pilot installations, with full approval expected in the coming months. Additional utility approvals are expected soon. See the full list on the Enphase website.
The IQ Meter Collar is a compact microgrid interconnection device that mounts behind the utility meter or on a standalone meter socket. It enables whole-home backup without moving circuits to a dedicated backup sub-panel or installing additional consumption current transformers, while providing safe grid isolation. As a key component of the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, alongside the IQ® Battery 10C and the IQ® Combiner 6C, it helps reduce equipment, wiring complexity, and installation time. With integrated metering and streamlined commissioning, the system helps installers complete more installations in a single day and is backed by a 15-year limited warranty.
"Utility approval of the Enphase meter collar opens the door for us to deploy whole-home backup at much greater scale,” said Dan Moncayo, owner of HPM Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Southern California. "The IQ Meter Collar significantly simplifies installation, reduces equipment on the wall, and helps us deliver a cleaner, faster experience for homeowners while meeting utility requirements.”
"With SMUD approving the IQ Meter Collar, we now have a streamlined way to offer whole-home backup that aligns with local utility standards,” said Ed Murray, president of Aztec Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Northern California. "It allows us to complete installations more efficiently and expand access to reliable home energy systems for more customers.”

"Hawaii has one of the highest electricity rates in the country and a real need for resilient, whole-home backup,” said Cruz Romero, owner of Hi Power Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Hawaii. "The IQ Meter Collar gives us a faster, cleaner way to deliver that to homeowners across the islands, with less equipment on the wall and fewer steps in the install.”
"With utility approval of the IQ Meter Collar now in place, we're able to accelerate battery deployments across our service territory in ways we couldn't before,” said Kent Harle, CEO of Stellar Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in San Diego. "In markets like San Diego, where programs like the San Diego Community Power Solar Battery Savings program are creating real financial incentives for homeowners, having a faster, simpler installation solution means we can help more customers take advantage of those opportunities before they're gone.”
"Getting utility approval for the IQ Meter Collar has opened up a whole new level of service for our customers,” said Jeff Long, president and CEO of Infinium Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in the PG&E service territory. "We can now offer whole-home backup with a simpler installation process, which means faster deployments and a better experience for homeowners.”
"Utility approvals are critical to scaling whole-home backup,” said Ken Fong, senior vice president of sales at Enphase Energy. "With the IQ Meter Collar now approved by 80 utilities, we are removing a key barrier to battery adoption, enabling installers to bring our 4th-generation Enphase Energy System to more homeowners, faster and more efficiently.”
For more information about the IQ Meter Collar and the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, please visit the Enphase website.
About Enphase Energy, Inc.
Enphase Energy, a global energy technology company based in Fremont, CA, is the world's leading supplier of microinverter-based solar and battery systems, EV chargers, home energy management systems, and virtual power plant (VPP) solutions. Solar Stocks Slide as High Borrowing Costs Weigh on Project Financing: First Solar Sinks 8%, SolarEdge Falls 5%, Enphase Energy Drops 4%
Rising borrowing costs are hitting solar stocks harder than almost anything else in the market Thursday, and the reasons behind the selloff reveal deeper vulnerabilities across the entire renewable energy sector.
Published September 24, 2026, 11:55am ET · 4 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A landscape featuring solar panels and wind turbines, representing the clean energy assets central to companies like NextEra Energy and Brookfield Renewable Partners, which are increasingly attractive to dividend investors. © hrui / iStock via Getty Images
Solar stocks are sliding sharply Thursday as elevated borrowing costs add pressure to an industry that depends heavily on project financing. First Solar (NASDAQ:FSLR | FSLR Price Prediction) stock is down 8% to $177.45, while SolarEdge Technologies (NASDAQ:SEDG) stock is falling 5% to $31.76 and Enphase Energy (NASDAQ:ENPH) stock is down 3% to $32.04.
The selling is broad across the solar industry, with Invesco Solar ETF (NYSE ARCA:TAN) down 4% to $43.23 while SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) is down 0.54% to $763.69. Higher interest rates can make new solar installations and upgrades more difficult to finance, potentially slowing private investment even when demand for renewable power remains intact.
Solar projects often require substantial upfront capital before generating revenue or reducing energy costs, making financing conditions particularly important for First Solar, SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. Higher borrowing costs can raise the required return on new projects and make some planned installations less attractive to developers, businesses and homeowners.
First Solar stock is facing the steepest decline among the three major solar names Thursday, although the immediate catalyst remains unclear. The broader weakness in First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock suggests that investors are also responding to macroeconomic concerns rather than a single company-specific development.
The financing pressure can affect different parts of the solar industry in different ways. First Solar supplies utility-scale solar modules, while SolarEdge and Enphase Energy provide technologies used in solar installations, meaning higher financing costs can ultimately affect equipment demand if developers delay projects or customers reduce spending.
First Solar has benefited from U.S. manufacturing incentives and demand for domestically produced solar modules, but First Solar stock can still be sensitive to changes in clean-energy policy and project economics. First Solar’s large utility-scale exposure also means financing conditions can influence the timing of projects even when the long-term demand outlook remains constructive.
Another issue surrounding First Solar is the company’s decision to withdraw its Section 337 complaint involving certain TOPCon solar manufacturers. The move has generated discussion among traders about competitive conditions in the solar-module market, although the immediate relationship between the legal development and Thursday’s First Solar stock decline isn’t clear.
First Solar’s position as a major U.S. solar manufacturer gives First Solar a different business profile from SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. That distinction could matter as investors weigh the effects of financing costs, U.S. clean-energy incentives, module pricing and project demand across the solar industry.
SolarEdge stock is down 5% to $31.76 as the broader solar selloff continues. SolarEdge has faced a difficult operating environment as residential solar demand, inventory levels and financing conditions have pressured the solar equipment market.
Enphase Energy stock is also under pressure, falling 3% to $32.04 despite Enphase Energy’s focus on microinverters, batteries and energy-management systems. Higher financing costs could make residential and commercial solar-plus-storage installations less attractive at the margin, particularly when customers are already weighing higher equipment and borrowing costs.
The weakness in SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock also highlights the difference between equipment suppliers and utility-scale manufacturers. SolarEdge and Enphase Energy can be affected by installation volumes and customer financing conditions, while First Solar can be more directly exposed to the economics and timing of large utility-scale projects.
Policy And Market Concerns Add To Selling
U.S. clean-energy policy remains another source of uncertainty for First Solar, SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. Changes to tax credits and other incentives could alter project economics, while uncertainty can cause developers and customers to delay investment decisions as they assess the financial benefits of new solar installations.
The 4% decline in the Invesco Solar ETF puts Thursday’s weakness into broader industry context, while the smaller 0.54% decline in the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust suggests solar stocks are experiencing substantially more pressure than the wider market. Investors can watch for signs that higher borrowing costs are slowing project commitments, while First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock could also respond to changes in policy, demand and financing conditions.
The combination of elevated interest rates, policy uncertainty and company-specific concerns leaves the solar sector with several factors to balance. Investors should consider keeping their position sizes modest as First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock remain sensitive to financing conditions and shifts in expectations for renewable-energy investment.

extended a run of product and manufacturing announcements this week even as its shares slid in a broad solar selloff. The company said its meter collar has now won approval from a growing list of utilities across the United States and Canada, and it began domestic production of power modules aimed at artificial intelligence data centers.
The share price move reflected sector-wide pressure rather than a single company disclosure. Higher borrowing costs have hit residential solar particularly hard, because homeowners frequently finance rooftop systems through loans and leases whose monthly payments rise when interest rates climb.
Against that backdrop, the announcements highlight a company trying to widen its addressable market beyond conventional rooftop solar. Backup power, grid services, and electrification of data centers represent adjacent areas where its power electronics expertise could find new uses.
A Residential Solar Market Under Financial Strain
Household solar demand across the United States has cooled as financing has become more expensive and as changes to federal tax credits alter the economics for homeowners. Installers have reported slower conversations, longer sales cycles, and greater price sensitivity among customers weighing whether to add panels.
Microinverters, the core product of Enphase Energy, convert direct current from each individual panel into usable alternating current at the roof. They are sold mainly through installers and distributors, so the company's fortunes track the health of the installer community closely.
When rates rise, smaller installers can struggle to keep cash flowing, and larger firms may pause expansion. Market participants have therefore treated microinverter suppliers as a sensitive gauge of the residential solar cycle, and recent share performance reflects that sensitivity.
Meter Collar Approvals Open Doors to Whole-Home Backup
The company's meter collar is a device installed between the utility meter and the meter socket, enabling a home battery and solar system to connect to the grid and to operate during outages without extensive rewiring. Approval by individual utilities is a necessary step before installers can offer the product in that service territory.
Each new approval expands the number of households that can reach whole-home backup solutions from the company. Utilities review interconnection and safety characteristics carefully, so a longer list of approvals signals growing acceptance among the gatekeepers of the grid.
Backup power has emerged as a compelling reason for homeowners to add batteries, especially in regions prone to storms, wildfires, and grid strain. Products that simplify installation and lower labor costs may help installers offset weaker demand for solar-only systems.
Data Center Power Hardware Marks a Strategic Pivot
The most notable development is the company's move into power hardware for data centers. Enphase Energy began domestic production of power modules destined for solid-state transformer racks, a technology that promises more efficient conversion of grid electricity to the direct current used by servers and accelerators.
Artificial intelligence facilities consume vast amounts of electricity and demand extremely reliable, dense power delivery. Traditional transformers and rectifiers take up space and lose energy during conversion, so engineers have been exploring solid-state approaches built from advanced semiconductors.
Enphase Energy has spent years mastering compact, high-efficiency power conversion for rooftops. Applying similar engineering to data center racks is a logical extension, although the customer base, sales cycle, and qualification process differ greatly from the residential market.
Manufacturing the new modules in American facilities aligns with growing customer demand for domestically sourced electrical equipment. Large technology firms and data center developers face scrutiny of supply chains and are attentive to tariff exposure and delivery reliability.
Federal incentives for domestic manufacturing of clean energy components also shape the economics. The company has previously worked with contract manufacturers in several American states to produce microinverters, taking advantage of tax credits tied to domestic production.
Ramping a new product line requires careful coordination with partners, and early volumes are typically modest. Market participants will look for evidence that production is scaling smoothly and that early customers are moving from prototypes to sustained orders.
Market Reaction and Sentiment Around the Stock
Shares fell notably on the day and have dropped sharply over recent months, trading well below the highs of the past year and closer to the lower end of the yearly range. Commentary has been mixed, with some observers calling the stock undervalued on certain screens and others citing weakening demand and competitive pressure.
Wall Street sentiment on the name has drifted toward the cautious side, with a consensus that leans neutral and a few voices turning more negative because of declining revenue, market share concerns, and pressure on unit economics. Others argue that the business retains strong technology and brand recognition.
Such divergent views are typical of companies in transition. Market participants alike are trying to judge whether new markets can offset softness in the core residential business, and that judgment will play out over many quarters rather than in a single announcement cycle.
Competitive Landscape in Inverters and Storage
Competition in residential solar electronics is fierce. Rivals include string inverter makers, integrated battery and solar providers, and vertically integrated installers that design their own equipment. Price competition has intensified as Chinese suppliers offer lower-cost alternatives in many global markets.
Enphase Energy competes by emphasizing reliability, software, and a complete home energy system that includes microinverters, batteries, and electric vehicle chargers. Its monitoring platform gives installers and homeowners visibility into system performance, adding a layer of stickiness.
In the data center arena, the competitive set differs. Established power electronics manufacturers and large industrial suppliers already serve hyperscale customers, so the company will need to demonstrate performance advantages and manufacturing reliability to win meaningful business.
Tax Credit Changes and Their Ripple Effects
Changes to federal residential solar tax credits have altered customer economics. When incentives shrink or expire for certain ownership structures, installers shift toward leasing arrangements, third-party ownership, or alternative financing to preserve demand, each with implications for equipment volumes.
Manufacturers like Enphase Energy tend to see order patterns shift ahead of deadlines, with pull-forward activity followed by digestion periods. This can make quarterly results choppy and complicates efforts to read underlying demand trends.
Regulatory uncertainty also affects installer confidence. Companies in the industry are watching guidance from federal agencies and legislative developments for clues about how long incentives will last and what conditions will apply to domestic content.
Power Demand From Artificial Intelligence Reshapes the Grid
Electricity consumption by data centers has become one of the defining themes in energy markets. Utilities are planning for large increases in load, and technology companies are exploring on-site generation, batteries, and more efficient power architectures to keep facilities running.
Efficiency gains at the rack level matter because even small improvements in conversion losses can translate to meaningful savings when multiplied across enormous campuses. This creates an opening for suppliers with strong power semiconductor design capabilities.
For Enphase Energy, this trend offers a narrative beyond rooftop solar. Whether the company can turn interest into consistent revenue remains unproven, but the direction of travel in data center design gives management a credible story to tell.
Management has been prioritizing cost discipline, inventory management, and channel health as demand has softened. Reducing excess inventory at distributors and installers helps keep pricing stable and prevents disruptive discounting later.
Product development continues on next-generation microinverters, bidirectional electric vehicle charging, and battery systems that can supply the grid during peak periods. These offerings aim to make the home a flexible energy asset rather than simply a solar generator.
International markets add diversity. Europe and other regions have their own incentives and installation patterns, and the company has been adapting products to local grid codes. Performance abroad can offset some domestic weakness, though currency swings and regional rule changes add complexity.
The company's share performance illustrates how differently pieces of the energy stocks universe respond to the same macro forces. Rising bond yields squeeze rate-sensitive renewable names, while midstream infrastructure operators benefit from steady contracted volumes and rising power-related gas demand.
Market participants often group solar, storage, and grid equipment together, yet business models diverge widely. Residential solar suppliers depend on consumer credit conditions, while data center suppliers depend on the capital spending plans of large technology firms.
Broader indexes such as the Nasdaq Composite have been led by semiconductor and artificial intelligence strength, and the company's pivot toward data center hardware seeks to connect its story to that momentum, even while its core residential business faces headwinds.
Persistent challenges include higher financing costs, uncertain incentives, slower installer activity, and pricing pressure from lower-cost competitors. Interconnection queues and permitting delays can also lengthen project timelines for residential and commercial systems alike.
Inventory dynamics remain a concern. Channel destocking cycles can depress reported revenue for several quarters, complicating efforts to gauge end-market demand. Companies must manage production carefully to avoid both shortages and gluts.
Diversification carries its own hazards. Entering the data center market demands new engineering resources, customer relationships, and qualification efforts, and results may take time to materialize. Missteps could distract from core operations during a difficult period.
Software and Services as a Second Engine
Beyond hardware, Enphase Energy has built a software platform that lets homeowners monitor production, manage batteries, and participate in grid programs. Recurring engagement through an app keeps the company connected to end customers long after an installer completes a project.

Enphase Energy Announces IQ Meter Collar Approval by 80 Utilities in the U.S. and Canada
FREMONT, Calif., Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today announced that the Enphase® IQ® Meter Collar is now approved for behind-the-meter installation by 80 utilities that collectively serve more than 38 million customers across the United States and Canada.
The IQ Meter Collar is now approved by all three major investor-owned electric utilities in California and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), expanding access to whole-home backup across the state. Hawaiian Electric has also approved initial pilot installations, with full approval expected in the coming months. Additional utility approvals are expected soon. See the full list on the Enphase website.
The IQ Meter Collar is a compact microgrid interconnection device that mounts behind the utility meter or on a standalone meter socket. It enables whole-home backup without moving circuits to a dedicated backup sub-panel or installing additional consumption current transformers, while providing safe grid isolation. As a key component of the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, alongside the IQ® Battery 10C and the IQ® Combiner 6C, it helps reduce equipment, wiring complexity, and installation time. With integrated metering and streamlined commissioning, the system helps installers complete more installations in a single day and is backed by a 15-year limited warranty.
“Utility approval of the Enphase meter collar opens the door for us to deploy whole-home backup at much greater scale,” said Dan Moncayo, owner of HPM Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Southern California. “The IQ Meter Collar significantly simplifies installation, reduces equipment on the wall, and helps us deliver a cleaner, faster experience for homeowners while meeting utility requirements.”
“With SMUD approving the IQ Meter Collar, we now have a streamlined way to offer whole-home backup that aligns with local utility standards,” said Ed Murray, president of Aztec Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Northern California. “It allows us to complete installations more efficiently and expand access to reliable home energy systems for more customers.”
“Hawaii has one of the highest electricity rates in the country and a real need for resilient, whole-home backup,” said Cruz Romero, owner of Hi Power Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Hawaii. “The IQ Meter Collar gives us a faster, cleaner way to deliver that to homeowners across the islands, with less equipment on the wall and fewer steps in the install.”
“With utility approval of the IQ Meter Collar now in place, we're able to accelerate battery deployments across our service territory in ways we couldn't before,” said Kent Harle, CEO of Stellar Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in San Diego. “In markets like San Diego, where programs like the San Diego Community Power Solar Battery Savings program are creating real financial incentives for homeowners, having a faster, simpler installation solution means we can help more customers take advantage of those opportunities before they're gone.”
“Getting utility approval for the IQ Meter Collar has opened up a whole new level of service for our customers,” said Jeff Long, president and CEO of Infinium Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in the PG&E service territory. “We can now offer whole-home backup with a simpler installation process, which means faster deployments and a better experience for homeowners.”
“Utility approvals are critical to scaling whole-home backup,” said Ken Fong, senior vice president of sales at Enphase Energy. “With the IQ Meter Collar now approved by 80 utilities, we are removing a key barrier to battery adoption, enabling installers to bring our 4th-generation Enphase Energy System to more homeowners, faster and more efficiently.”
For more information about the IQ Meter Collar and the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, please visit the Enphase website.
About Enphase Energy, Inc.
Enphase Energy, a global energy technology company based in Fremont, CA, is the world's leading supplier of microinverter-based solar and battery systems, EV chargers, home energy management systems, and virtual power plant (VPP) solutions. Enphase products enable people to harness the sun to make, use, save, and sell their own power, all controlled through the Enphase App. The company revolutionized the solar industry with its microinverter-based technology and has shipped approximately 89.4 million microinverters, with approximately 5.3 million Enphase-based systems deployed in over 165 countries. Enphase Energy Drops 5% as Solar Selling Resumes; First Solar and Sunrun Fall 4%
Solar names bounced hard on Thursday, but that relief trade collapsed by Friday morning, and now one question hangs over the sector: whether the rate path has already decided where these stocks go next.
Published September 18, 2026, 1:01pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Enphase Energy (NASDAQ:ENPH | ENPH Price Prediction) is sliding again on Friday, giving back part of a bounce that formed earlier in the week. The Invesco Solar ETF (NYSEARCA:TAN) is down 2%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down only 0.2%, so the selling is concentrated in solar rather than spread across the broad market.
ENPH stock is at $34.29, down 5% in Friday morning trading. That leaves Enphase Energy stock up 7% year to date (YTD), so today’s move clips a gain rather than deepens an existing hole.
Meanwhile, First Solar (NASDAQ:FSLR) stock is at $193.38, down 4%, part of the same sector move. Sunrun (NASDAQ:RUN) stock is at $8.40, down 4%, extending a much longer slide for the residential installer.
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates this week, its first increase in three years, and left the door open to another. Residential solar is financed rather than bought outright in most cases, which puts the cost of a loan directly underneath demand for home systems. That mechanism is the standing reason Enphase Energy trades on the rate path, and it explains why a macro headline can move the stock as sharply as a company release.
Enphase Energy’s residential microinverter and battery business is exposed to that dynamic more directly than a utility-scale competitor would be. When borrowing costs rise, homeowners defer or scale back the systems that carry Enphase Energy’s hardware, and the demand signal into its channel softens with them. That knock-on effect eventually shows up in shipments, sell-through and channel inventory.
Enphase Energy isn’t falling on its own today. First Solar and Sunrun are also lower, the Invesco Solar ETF slid alongside them, and the broad market barely moved. Any name in this group carries the same headline risk from the rate path, and Enphase Energy happens to be the biggest mover in the session.
24/7 Wall St. reported on Thursday that solar names rose as an earlier selloff in the group unwound. That advance hasn’t held into Friday, and Enphase Energy is giving back the largest share of it.
One feature separates Enphase Energy from the rest of the group. Enphase Energy stock is still higher on the year, so today’s selling clips a gain instead of deepening an existing hole the way it does at First Solar and Sunrun. That cushion is thin, however, and it doesn’t alter the source of the pressure on Enphase Energy.
The harder problem for Enphase Energy is that a demand story resting on financing costs doesn’t improve until the rate path does. Until borrowing conditions ease, the residential business at the center of Enphase Energy’s revenue mix stays under the same weight that pulled the stock lower on Friday.
Investors can watch for whether the Invesco Solar ETF holds through the close, since a break lower could drag Enphase Energy further with it. An advance in the same fund could lift Enphase Energy in kind, given how tightly the two names have tracked in this session.
For investors adding new exposure to Enphase Energy, a cautious posture makes sense while the sector trades on macro conditions rather than on company fundamentals. Trimming their positions, or waiting for a clearer read on borrowing costs, should keep their risk in line with a name whose demand backdrop remains tied to the rate cycle.

Fresh interest in Enphase Energy is tied to residential solar demand and channel inventory. Investors are likely to separate a credible operating advance from enthusiasm borrowed from the wider sector.
Readers following Energy Stocks can use the present move as a starting point, while keeping the analysis tied to Enphase Energy's own disclosures and business conditions.
The strongest version of the argument depends on execution that customers can see. For Enphase Energy, that means clearer demand signals, disciplined spending and progress in the part of the business linked to residential solar demand. A broad market tailwind can help sentiment, but it cannot replace evidence from the company itself.
The broader energy stocks group is not moving as one block. Companies with dependable balance sheets and clear catalysts are receiving a different response from businesses that rely mainly on a sector narrative. Enphase Energy therefore has to earn its own place in the trade. Its listing in the Nasdaq Composite provides market context, but index direction alone says little about company-specific execution.
Uncertainty remains around timing. A company can be directionally right and still disappoint if product delivery, approvals, integration or customer uptake arrives slowly. For Enphase Energy, the next stage will be judged on specificity. Ambiguous language or shifting priorities would make it harder to distinguish a real improvement from a temporary change in sentiment.
Another useful lens is the quality of the decision facing customers. A purchase linked to residential solar demand may involve budget approval, technical integration or a change in everyday behavior. That makes the sales path as important as the product claim. Enphase Energy can improve confidence by showing that customers return, expand their use or commit after an initial trial. If engagement remains narrow, the market may question whether the opportunity is large enough to support expectations.
For ENPH, a sensible watchlist includes customer traction, competitive behavior, capital allocation and the quality of management's guidance. None of those items should be read in isolation. Together they will show whether the company is building a repeatable advantage or simply benefiting from the present market theme.
The current setup makes Enphase Energy worth following, but patience remains part of the analysis. A durable re-rating would require a clearer link between residential solar demand and the quality of the underlying business. Until that evidence arrives, the stock is best viewed through a balanced lens: open to improvement, alert to execution risk.

The market is reassessing residential solar demand and channel inventory. The important issue is whether the attention is supported by company-specific execution.

Because Enphase Energy is listed on NASDAQ, the broad exchange context used here is [Nasdaq Composite]. This does not imply membership in a narrower benchmark.

Watch the next company release for concrete information on demand, delivery, spending discipline and the operating priorities linked to residential solar demand and channel inventory.

Here is What to Know Beyond Why Enphase Energy, Inc. (ENPH) is a Trending Stock
Fri, October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT 5 min read
Enphase Energy (ENPH) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.
Over the past month, shares of this solar technology company have returned -9.6%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +0.6% change. During this period, the Zacks Solar industry, which Enphase Energy falls in, has lost 9.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?
Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.
Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.
Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.
Enphase Energy is expected to post earnings of $0.48 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of -46.7%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged.
The consensus earnings estimate of $1.93 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of -34.8%. This estimate has remained unchanged over the last 30 days.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.39 indicates a change of +23.5% from what Enphase Energy is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.
Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Enphase Energy is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for ENPH
While earnings growth is arguably the most superior indicator of a company's financial health, nothing happens as such if a business isn't able to grow its revenues. After all, it's nearly impossible for a company to increase its earnings for an extended period without increasing its revenues. So, it's important to know a company's potential revenue growth.
For Enphase Energy, the consensus sales estimate for the current quarter of $306.7 million indicates a year-over-year change of -25.3%. For the current and next fiscal years, $1.19 billion and $1.32 billion estimates indicate -19% and +10.3% changes, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Enphase Energy reported revenues of $291.85 million in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of -19.6%. EPS of $0.46 for the same period compares with $0.69 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $292.17 million, the reported revenues represent a surprise of -0.11%. The EPS surprise was 0%.
Over the last four quarters, Enphase Energy surpassed consensus EPS estimates three times. The company topped consensus revenue estimates two times over this period.
No investment decision can be efficient without considering a stock's valuation. Whether a stock's current price rightly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects is an essential determinant of its future price performance.
Comparing the current value of a company's valuation multiples, such as its price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), to its own historical values helps ascertain whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, whereas comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of how reasonable its stock price is.
The Zacks Value Style Score (part of the Zacks Style Scores system), which pays close attention to both traditional and unconventional valuation metrics to grade stocks from A to F (an A is better than a B; a B is better than a C; and so on), is pretty helpful in identifying whether a stock is overvalued, rightly valued, or temporarily undervalued.
Enphase Energy is graded D on this front, indicating that it is trading at a premium to its peers. Click here to see the values of some of the valuation metrics that have driven this grade.
The facts discussed here and much other information on Zacks.com might help determine whether or not it's worthwhile paying attention to the market buzz about Enphase Energy. However, its Zacks Rank #3 does suggest that it may perform in line with the broader market in the near term.

pages.title: Enphase Energy Rises 5% as Solid-State Transformer Modules Enter Texas Production, SolarEdge Jumps 6% - 24/7 Wall St.
pages.text:
Enphase Energy Rises 5% as Solid-State Transformer Modules Enter Texas Production, SolarEdge Jumps 6%
A Texas factory just handed Enphase a credible claim on the AI data-center power market, and SolarEdge surged even harder despite announcing nothing at all.
Published September 8, 2026, 12:49pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Vast fields of solar panels and wind turbines symbolize the booming clean energy sector, a key driver behind the ALPS Clean Energy ETF's recent strong performance. © Piyaset / Shutterstock.com
Solar names caught a midday bid on a manufacturing milestone tied to AI data-center power infrastructure. Enphase Energy (NASDAQ:ENPH | ENPH Price Prediction) said power modules for its IQ Solid-State Transformer, or IQ SST, are now being built at its Arlington, Texas facility, enabling full-scale racks to be assembled and validated for prospective data-center customers. SolarEdge Technologies (NASDAQ:SEDG) stock rallied in sympathy, boosted by its own SST platform aimed at the same AI-factory opportunity.
The Invesco Solar ETF (NYSEARCA:TAN) is up 3% on the session. Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.42%, framing solar as a clear day-of outperformer against a softer broad-market tape.
Enphase stock is up 5% to $38.31, extending its year-to-date gain to 20%. At the same time, SolarEdge stock is climbing 6% to $36.34, an outsized reaction given that the company hasn’t announced any news of its own today.
Texas Line Puts a Face on the AI-Power Pitch
Each IQ SST power module is rated at 4 kW, and hundreds combine into a rack with capacity up to 5 MW. The design converts medium-voltage AC (13.8 kV or 34.5 kV) directly to 800-volt DC, with sub-millisecond response to the sharp load swings AI training and inference workloads generate, reducing the need for battery buffering next to every compute rack.
Co-founder and chief product officer Raghu Belur explained that hundreds of modules together make a multi-megawatt rack, and Enphase scales by repeating the same compact module rather than building larger power-conversion systems. The modules share their form factor and production process with the company’s microinverters, which makes the Texas milestone credible rather than a paper design.
Enphase’s management flagged customer engagement across hyperscalers, neoclouds, colocation providers, EPCs, and server providers, with opportunities at the RFI and RFP stages representing potential demand totaling multiple gigawatts. Full-system demonstrations remain on track for later this year, with customer pilots beginning in 2027 and commercial shipments in 2028.
SolarEdge’s own SST platform targets the same AI-factory build-out, and CEO Shuki Nir has framed the effort as addressing “the significant opportunity in AI factories.” On the company’s August 5 earnings call, SolarEdge said prospective customer engineering teams viewed a working prototype convert medium-voltage AC to a regulated 800-volt DC bus at 99% efficiency across a range of power levels.
SolarEdge’s roadmap points to a working lab system by the end of 2026, pilot installations in 2027, and volume shipments in 2028, mirroring Enphase’s commercialization schedule. Both names remain pre-revenue on the data-center side, and SolarEdge’s investor day on September 10, 2026 sits two days out as its next scheduled disclosure moment.
First Solar (NASDAQ:FSLR), the largest U.S. solar manufacturer, sits outside the SST story, though its 45.1-gigawatt contracted backlog through 2030 keeps it central to any broader rotation into domestic solar. First Solar stock is down 19% year to date, entering today’s sector move from a much weaker anchor than its two rallying sector peers.
The Invesco Solar ETF’s 3% session gain lags both SST-linked names by a wide margin, suggesting today’s bid is concentrated in the two companies with an explicit AI-data-center power narrative. That divergence underscores how selective the tape has been within the solar complex.
The AI-power thesis in solar names now has a factory address. A signed contract with a data-center operator remains ahead, and Enphase’s next tangible catalyst is a full-system IQ SST demonstration targeted for November, followed by customer pilots in 2027 and commercial shipments in 2028. SolarEdge’s Thursday investor day could validate today’s sympathy bid with firmer numbers around its data-center opportunity.
The bulls can argue that Enphase’s Texas line proves a residential-solar manufacturer can credibly extend into medium-voltage data-center gear using its existing production base. The bears could counter that SolarEdge outran Enphase today on no company-specific news, suggesting part of the move is a sector-wide bid that could fade if AI-power sentiment cools.
Investors sizing their exposure should treat both names as speculative AI-adjacent positions rather than solar-industrial staples, keeping their allocations modest ahead of SolarEdge’s investor day and Enphase’s late-year system demonstration. Position sizing matters more than usual given the pre-revenue status of both SST platforms.

Enphase Energy (ENPH) Stock Looks Near Fair Value On Cash Flow
Enphase Energy has seen its stock fall a long way over the past few years, which puts fresh focus on whether the current price lines up with the cash the business can generate. After that kind of reset, many investors naturally ask if the share price now reflects the company's underlying cash flows or if the market is still out of sync.
Over the past 5 years, Enphase Energy's share price has declined 79.1%, which raises the question of how much of its cash flow potential is already being discounted.
Approval of the IQ Meter Collar by 80 utilities across the U.S. and Canada may support expectations for future battery deployments, which can influence how steady and sizable Enphase Energy's cash flows look over time.

Does Enphase Energy Look Fairly Valued on Cash Flow?
The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here is built around Enphase Energy's ability to turn its business into free cash for shareholders. On the latest twelve-month view, the company produced about $156.8 million of free cash flow, and the forecast path assumes those cash flows recover and grow over time rather than fade. That projection uses a two-stage setup, with an initial ramp in free cash generation followed by flatter, more mature levels further out.
Those assumptions leave the DCF outcome broadly in line with the current share price of $32.40, so the market is effectively giving Enphase Energy credit for the cash flow profile embedded in these projections rather than a deep discount or a big premium. Because the IQ Meter Collar has now been cleared by 80 utilities across the U.S. and Canada, the prospect of more battery deployments helps explain why investors appear comfortable valuing the shares around what this cash flow model suggests. pages.text:

Enphase (ENPH) Wins 80 Utility Approvals. Can Easier Installation Boost Battery Sales?
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) reported on September 21 that 80 utilities across the United States and Canada had approved its IQ Meter Collar for installation behind the electricity meter. Those utilities collectively serve more than 38 million customers, expanding access to a simpler way of connecting home battery backup systems.
For Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH), the opportunity is to turn easier installation into additional battery sales. The device allows a home to disconnect safely from the grid during backup operation. Broader approval makes the product available in more service territories, while completed projects will determine the financial benefit.
Don't Miss: Enphase (ENPH) is Preparing for the End of Dutch Net Metering. Will It Boost Batteries or Hurt Solar Demand?
Enphase Energy (ENPH) Surges 12.83% as Senators Rethink Clean Energy Credit Cuts
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) says the IQ Meter Collar eliminates the need to move circuits into a separate backup panel or add separate hardware to monitor electricity consumption. Less wiring and equipment can reduce installation work. Installers could use those savings to offer more competitive proposals or complete more projects with the same crews.
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) now has approvals from California's three major investor-owned electric utilities and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District. That gives installers a broader geographic base for offering the simplified installation. The commercial advantage would strengthen if fewer installation complications helped convert homeowner interest into firm orders.
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) shipped 113.8 megawatt-hours of batteries in the second quarter, up from 103.1 in the first quarter, an increase of approximately 10.4%. More than 25,000 installers worldwide were certified to install its batteries. That existing installer network gives the company a foundation for expanding adoption as utility access improves.
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) still needs homeowners to commit money. The 38 million figure measures customers served by the utilities, not battery orders or a count of suitable homes. Installation savings address only part of the purchase decision. Financing costs, electricity bills and the value homeowners place on backup power will influence demand.
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) also faces differences in approval status. Hawaiian Electric has approved initial pilot installations, with full approval expected in the coming months. Progress from pilot installations to broader availability will matter for that territory. Installers must also execute reliably enough for simpler system design to translate into shorter project timelines.
Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) did not quantify average installation savings or expected incremental revenue in the announcement. Faster installation could improve installer margins without generating many additional sales. Battery shipment growth will therefore need to be considered alongside completed installations, customer demand, and pricing to establish whether the approvals create lasting value.
The filings available so far reflect positions held before Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) reported its IQ Meter Collar approvals from 80 utilities. Insider Monkey's database showed 50 hedge funds holding Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENPH) at the end of 2Q2026.

First Solar, Enphase, SolarEdge, Alight, and Goodyear Shares Are Falling, What You Need To Know
First Solar, Enphase, SolarEdge, Alight, and Goodyear Shares Are Falling, What You Need To Know
What Happened?
A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 5.14%, reaching levels last seen in 2007 and raising borrowing costs across the economy. U.S. stocks fell early Thursday, according to the Associated Press, as surging Treasury yields and rebounding energy prices weighed on financial markets.
A Treasury yield is the return investors earn for lending money to the U.S. government. The 10-year yield is closely watched because it serves as a benchmark for many other borrowing costs, including mortgages and corporate loans. When it rises, it becomes more expensive for households and businesses to borrow, which can slow spending and investment. Higher yields can also make stocks look less attractive. When investors can earn a relatively safe return of more than 5% from government bonds, some may choose to move money out of riskier assets such as equities.
Companies that depend on borrowing to fund growth, or whose value is based heavily on expected future profits, often feel this pressure most. Rebounding energy prices added to the strain. Higher fuel costs can raise expenses for businesses and consumers and may keep inflation elevated, which could keep upward pressure on interest rates. Taken together, the jump in yields to their highest level in roughly two decades and the rise in energy prices created a difficult backdrop for stocks across the sector, with many companies moving lower together.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

The biggest move we wrote about over the last year was about 2 months ago when the stock dropped 17% on the news that the company's weak forward guidance overshadowed its better-than-expected second-quarter revenue and profitability. While Alight's second-quarter revenue and adjusted profitability came in ahead of estimates, investors focused on the company's 3.2% year-over-year sales decline and deteriorating outlook.
Looking ahead, management offered cautious guidance, projecting third-quarter revenue to be 5.5% below analyst expectations at a midpoint of $2.09 Billion.
Furthermore, the company's full-year forecasts for both revenue and adjusted EBITDA also fell short of consensus estimates, signaling ongoing challenges for the business.

Enphase Energy, Inc. (ENPH) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know
Enphase Energy (ENPH) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.
Over the past month, shares of this solar technology company have returned -10.3%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -1.3% change. During this period, the Zacks Solar industry, which Enphase Energy falls in, has lost 10.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?
Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
For the current quarter, Enphase Energy is expected to post earnings of $0.48 per share, indicating a change of -46.7% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged over the last 30 days.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $1.93 points to a change of -34.8% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has remained unchanged.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.39 indicates a change of +23.5% from what Enphase Energy is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.
Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Enphase Energy is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

While earnings growth is arguably the most superior indicator of a company's financial health, nothing happens as such if a business isn't able to grow its revenues. After all, it's nearly impossible for a company to increase its earnings for an extended period without increasing its revenues. So, it's important to know a company's potential revenue growth.
In the case of Enphase Energy, the consensus sales estimate of $306.7 million for the current quarter points to a year-over-year change of -25.3%. The $1.2 billion and $1.33 billion estimates for the current and next fiscal years indicate changes of -18.3% and +10.3%, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Enphase Energy reported revenues of $291.85 million in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of -19.6%. EPS of $0.46 for the same period compares with $0.69 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $292.17 million, the reported revenues represent a surprise of -0.11%. The EPS surprise was 0%.
Over the last four quarters, Enphase Energy surpassed consensus EPS estimates three times. The company topped consensus revenue estimates two times over this period.
Without considering a stock's valuation, no investment decision can be efficient. In predicting a stock's future price performance, it's crucial to determine whether its current price correctly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects.
Comparing the current value of a company's valuation multiples, such as its price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), to its own historical values helps ascertain whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, whereas comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of how reasonable its stock price is.
The Zacks Value Style Score (part of the Zacks Style Scores system), which pays close attention to both traditional and unconventional valuation metrics to grade stocks from A to F (an A is better than a B; a B is better than a C; and so on), is pretty helpful in identifying whether a stock is overvalued, rightly valued, or temporarily undervalued.
Enphase Energy is graded D on this front, indicating that it is trading at a premium to its peers. Click here to see the values of some of the valuation metrics that have driven this grade.
The facts discussed here and much other information on Zacks.com might help determine whether or not it's worthwhile paying attention to the market buzz about Enphase Energy. However, its Zacks Rank #3 does suggest that it may perform in line with the broader market in the near term.

Enphase Energy Announces IQ Meter Collar Approval by 80 Utilities in the U.S. and Canada
Enphase Energy, Inc.
Enphase Energy, Inc.
FREMONT, Calif., Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enphase Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENPH), a global energy technology company, today announced that the Enphase® IQ® Meter Collar is now approved for behind-the-meter installation by 80 utilities that collectively serve more than 38 million customers across the United States and Canada.
The IQ Meter Collar is now approved by all three major investor-owned electric utilities in California and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), expanding access to whole-home backup across the state. Hawaiian Electric has also approved initial pilot installations, with full approval expected in the coming months. Additional utility approvals are expected soon. See the full list on the Enphase website.
The IQ Meter Collar is a compact microgrid interconnection device that mounts behind the utility meter or on a standalone meter socket. It enables whole-home backup without moving circuits to a dedicated backup sub-panel or installing additional consumption current transformers, while providing safe grid isolation. As a key component of the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, alongside the IQ® Battery 10C and the IQ® Combiner 6C, it helps reduce equipment, wiring complexity, and installation time. With integrated metering and streamlined commissioning, the system helps installers complete more installations in a single day and is backed by a 15-year limited warranty.
"Utility approval of the Enphase meter collar opens the door for us to deploy whole-home backup at much greater scale," said Dan Moncayo, owner of HPM Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Southern California. "The IQ Meter Collar significantly simplifies installation, reduces equipment on the wall, and helps us deliver a cleaner, faster experience for homeowners while meeting utility requirements."
"With SMUD approving the IQ Meter Collar, we now have a streamlined way to offer whole-home backup that aligns with local utility standards," said Ed Murray, president of Aztec Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Northern California. "It allows us to complete installations more efficiently and expand access to reliable home energy systems for more customers."
"Hawaii has one of the highest electricity rates in the country and a real need for resilient, whole-home backup," said Cruz Romero, owner of Hi Power Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in Hawaii. "The IQ Meter Collar gives us a faster, cleaner way to deliver that to homeowners across the islands, with less equipment on the wall and fewer steps in the install."
"With utility approval of the IQ Meter Collar now in place, we're able to accelerate battery deployments across our service territory in ways we couldn't before," said Kent Harle, CEO of Stellar Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in San Diego. "In markets like San Diego, where programs like the San Diego Community Power Solar Battery Savings program are creating real financial incentives for homeowners, having a faster, simpler installation solution means we can help more customers take advantage of those opportunities before they're gone."
"Getting utility approval for the IQ Meter Collar has opened up a whole new level of service for our customers," said Jeff Long, president and CEO of Infinium Solar, an installer of Enphase products based in the PG&E service territory. "We can now offer whole-home backup with a simpler installation process, which means faster deployments and a better experience for homeowners."
"Utility approvals are critical to scaling whole-home backup," said Ken Fong, senior vice president of sales at Enphase Energy. "With the IQ Meter Collar now approved by 80 utilities, we are removing a key barrier to battery adoption, enabling installers to bring our 4th-generation Enphase Energy System to more homeowners, faster and more efficiently."
For more information about the IQ Meter Collar and the 4th-generation Enphase Energy System, please visit the Enphase website.
About Enphase Energy, Inc.
Enphase Energy, a global energy technology company based in Fremont, CA, is the world's leading supplier of microinverter-based solar and battery systems, EV chargers, home energy management systems, and virtual power plant (VPP) solutions. Enphase products enable people to harness the sun to make, use, save, and sell their own power, all controlled through the Enphase App. The company revolutionized the solar industry with its microinverter-based technology and has shipped approximately 89.4 million microinverters, with approximately 5.3 million Enphase-based systems deployed in over 165 countries. Solar stocks are sliding sharply Thursday as elevated borrowing costs add pressure to an industry that depends heavily on project financing. First Solar (NASDAQ:FSLR | FSLR Price Prediction) stock is down 8% to $177.45, while SolarEdge Technologies (NASDAQ:SEDG) stock is falling 5% to $31.76 and Enphase Energy (NASDAQ:ENPH) stock is down 3% to $32.04.
The selling is broad across the solar industry, with Invesco Solar ETF (NYSE ARCA:TAN) down 4% to $43.23 while SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) is down 0.54% to $763.69. Higher interest rates can make new solar installations and upgrades more difficult to finance, potentially slowing private investment even when demand for renewable power remains intact.
Solar projects often require substantial upfront capital before generating revenue or reducing energy costs, making financing conditions particularly important for First Solar, SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. Higher borrowing costs can raise the required return on new projects and make some planned installations less attractive to developers, businesses and homeowners.
First Solar stock is facing the steepest decline among the three major solar names Thursday, although the immediate catalyst remains unclear. The broader weakness in First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock suggests that investors are also responding to macroeconomic concerns rather than a single company-specific development.
The financing pressure can affect different parts of the solar industry in different ways. First Solar supplies utility-scale solar modules, while SolarEdge and Enphase Energy provide technologies used in solar installations, meaning higher financing costs can ultimately affect equipment demand if developers delay projects or customers reduce spending.
First Solar has benefited from U.S. manufacturing incentives and demand for domestically produced solar modules, but First Solar stock can still be sensitive to changes in clean-energy policy and project economics. First Solar’s large utility-scale exposure also means financing conditions can influence the timing of projects even when the long-term demand outlook remains constructive.
Another issue surrounding First Solar is the company’s decision to withdraw its Section 337 complaint involving certain TOPCon solar manufacturers. The move has generated discussion among traders about competitive conditions in the solar-module market, although the immediate relationship between the legal development and Thursday’s First Solar stock decline isn’t clear.
First Solar’s position as a major U.S. solar manufacturer gives First Solar a different business profile from SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. That distinction could matter as investors weigh the effects of financing costs, U.S. clean-energy incentives, module pricing and project demand across the solar industry.
SolarEdge stock is down 5% to $31.76 as the broader solar selloff continues. SolarEdge has faced a difficult operating environment as residential solar demand, inventory levels and financing conditions have pressured the solar equipment market.
Enphase Energy stock is also under pressure, falling 3% to $32.04 despite Enphase Energy’s focus on microinverters, batteries and energy-management systems. Higher financing costs could make residential and commercial solar-plus-storage installations less attractive at the margin, particularly when customers are already weighing higher equipment and borrowing costs.
The weakness in SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock also highlights the difference between equipment suppliers and utility-scale manufacturers. SolarEdge and Enphase Energy can be affected by installation volumes and customer financing conditions, while First Solar can be more directly exposed to the economics and timing of large utility-scale projects.
Policy And Market Concerns Add To Selling
U.S. clean-energy policy remains another source of uncertainty for First Solar, SolarEdge and Enphase Energy. Changes to tax credits and other incentives could alter project economics, while uncertainty can cause developers and customers to delay investment decisions as they assess the financial benefits of new solar installations.
The 4% decline in the Invesco Solar ETF puts Thursday’s weakness into broader industry context, while the smaller 0.54% decline in the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust suggests solar stocks are experiencing substantially more pressure than the wider market. Investors can watch for signs that higher borrowing costs are slowing project commitments, while First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock could also respond to changes in policy, demand and financing conditions.
The combination of elevated interest rates, policy uncertainty and company-specific concerns leaves the solar sector with several factors to balance. Investors should consider keeping their position sizes modest as First Solar stock, SolarEdge stock and Enphase Energy stock remain sensitive to financing conditions and shifts in expectations for renewable-energy investment.

The share price move reflected sector-wide pressure rather than a single company disclosure. Higher borrowing costs have hit residential solar particularly hard, because homeowners frequently finance rooftop systems through loans and leases whose monthly payments rise when interest rates climb.
Against that backdrop, the announcements highlight a company trying to widen its addressable market beyond conventional rooftop solar. Backup power, grid services, and electrification of data centers represent adjacent areas where its power electronics expertise could find new uses.
A Residential Solar Market Under Financial Strain
Household solar demand across the United States has cooled as financing has become more expensive and as changes to federal tax credits alter the economics for homeowners. Installers have reported slower conversations, longer sales cycles, and greater price sensitivity among customers weighing whether to add panels.
Microinverters, the core product of Enphase Energy, convert direct current from each individual panel into usable alternating current at the roof. They are sold mainly through installers and distributors, so the company's fortunes track the health of the installer community closely.
When rates rise, smaller installers can struggle to keep cash flowing, and larger firms may pause expansion. Market participants have therefore treated microinverter suppliers as a sensitive gauge of the residential solar cycle, and recent share performance reflects that sensitivity.
Meter Collar Approvals Open Doors to Whole-Home Backup
The company's meter collar is a device installed between the utility meter and the meter socket, enabling a home battery and solar system to connect to the grid and to operate during outages without extensive rewiring. Approval by individual utilities is a necessary step before installers can offer the product in that service territory.
Each new approval expands the number of households that can reach whole-home backup solutions from the company. Utilities review interconnection and safety characteristics carefully, so a longer list of approvals signals growing acceptance among the gatekeepers of the grid.
Backup power has emerged as a compelling reason for homeowners to add batteries, especially in regions prone to storms, wildfires, and grid strain. Products that simplify installation and lower labor costs may help installers offset weaker demand for solar-only systems.
Data Center Power Hardware Marks a Strategic Pivot
The most notable development is the company's move into power hardware for data centers. Enphase Energy began domestic production of power modules destined for solid-state transformer racks, a technology that promises more efficient conversion of grid electricity to the direct current used by servers and accelerators.
Artificial intelligence facilities consume vast amounts of electricity and demand extremely reliable, dense power delivery. Traditional transformers and rectifiers take up space and lose energy during conversion, so engineers have been exploring solid-state approaches built from advanced semiconductors.
Enphase Energy has spent years mastering compact, high-efficiency power conversion for rooftops. Applying similar engineering to data center racks is a logical extension, although the customer base, sales cycle, and qualification process differ greatly from the residential market.
Manufacturing the new modules in American facilities aligns with growing customer demand for domestically sourced electrical equipment. Large technology firms and data center developers face scrutiny of supply chains and are attentive to tariff exposure and delivery reliability.
Federal incentives for domestic manufacturing of clean energy components also shape the economics. The company has previously worked with contract manufacturers in several American states to produce microinverters, taking advantage of tax credits tied to domestic production.
Ramping a new product line requires careful coordination with partners, and early volumes are typically modest. Market participants will look for evidence that production is scaling smoothly and that early customers are moving from prototypes to sustained orders.
Market Reaction and Sentiment Around the Stock
Shares fell notably on the day and have dropped sharply over recent months, trading well below the highs of the past year and closer to the lower end of the yearly range. Commentary has been mixed, with some observers calling the stock undervalued on certain screens and others citing weakening demand and competitive pressure.
Wall Street sentiment on the name has drifted toward the cautious side, with a consensus that leans neutral and a few voices turning more negative because of declining revenue, market share concerns, and pressure on unit economics. Others argue that the business retains strong technology and brand recognition.
Such divergent views are typical of companies in transition. Market participants alike are trying to judge whether new markets can offset softness in the core residential business, and that judgment will play out over many quarters rather than in a single announcement cycle.
Competitive Landscape in Inverters and Storage
Competition in residential solar electronics is fierce. Rivals include string inverter makers, integrated battery and solar providers, and vertically integrated installers that design their own equipment. Price competition has intensified as Chinese suppliers offer lower-cost alternatives in many global markets.
Enphase Energy competes by emphasizing reliability, software, and a complete home energy system that includes microinverters, batteries, and electric vehicle chargers. Its monitoring platform gives installers and homeowners visibility into system performance, adding a layer of stickiness.
In the data center arena, the competitive set differs. Established power electronics manufacturers and large industrial suppliers already serve hyperscale customers, so the company will need to demonstrate performance advantages and manufacturing reliability to win meaningful business.
Tax Credit Changes and Their Ripple Effects
Changes to federal residential solar tax credits have altered customer economics. When incentives shrink or expire for certain ownership structures, installers shift toward leasing arrangements, third-party ownership, or alternative financing to preserve demand, each with implications for equipment volumes.
Manufacturers like Enphase Energy tend to see order patterns shift ahead of deadlines, with pull-forward activity followed by digestion periods. This can make quarterly results choppy and complicates efforts to read underlying demand trends.
Regulatory uncertainty also affects installer confidence. Companies in the industry are watching guidance from federal agencies and legislative developments for clues about how long incentives will last and what conditions will apply to domestic content.
Power Demand From Artificial Intelligence Reshapes the Grid
Electricity consumption by data centers has become one of the defining themes in energy markets. Utilities are planning for large increases in load, and technology companies are exploring on-site generation, batteries, and more efficient power architectures to keep facilities running.
Efficiency gains at the rack level matter because even small improvements in conversion losses can translate to meaningful savings when multiplied across enormous campuses. This creates an opening for suppliers with strong power semiconductor design capabilities.
For Enphase Energy, this trend offers a narrative beyond rooftop solar. Whether the company can turn interest into consistent revenue remains unproven, but the direction of travel in data center design gives management a credible story to tell.
Management has been prioritizing cost discipline, inventory management, and channel health as demand has softened. Reducing excess inventory at distributors and installers helps keep pricing stable and prevents disruptive discounting later.
Product development continues on next-generation microinverters, bidirectional electric vehicle charging, and battery systems that can supply the grid during peak periods. These offerings aim to make the home a flexible energy asset rather than simply a solar generator.
International markets add diversity. Europe and other regions have their own incentives and installation patterns, and the company has been adapting products to local grid codes. Performance abroad can offset some domestic weakness, though currency swings and regional rule changes add complexity.
The company's share performance illustrates how differently pieces of the energy stocks universe respond to the same macro forces. Rising bond yields squeeze rate-sensitive renewable names, while midstream infrastructure operators benefit from steady contracted volumes and rising power-related gas demand.
Market participants often group solar, storage, and grid equipment together, yet business models diverge widely. Residential solar suppliers depend on consumer credit conditions, while data center suppliers depend on the capital spending plans of large technology firms.
Broader indexes such as the Nasdaq Composite have been led by semiconductor and artificial intelligence strength, and the company's pivot toward data center hardware seeks to connect its story to that momentum, even while its core residential business faces headwinds.
Persistent challenges include higher financing costs, uncertain incentives, slower installer activity, and pricing pressure from lower-cost competitors. Interconnection queues and permitting delays can also lengthen project timelines for residential and commercial systems alike.
Inventory dynamics remain a concern. Channel destocking cycles can depress reported revenue for several quarters, complicating efforts to gauge end-market demand. Companies must manage production carefully to avoid both shortages and gluts.
Diversification carries its own hazards. Entering the data center market demands new engineering resources, customer relationships, and qualification efforts, and results may take time to materialize. Missteps could distract from core operations during a difficult period.
Software and Services as a Second Engine
Beyond hardware, Enphase Energy has built a software platform that lets homeowners monitor production, manage batteries, and participate in grid programs. Recurring engagement through an app keeps the company connected to end customers long after an installer completes a project.
